chapter: New York, Philadelphia and Harlem nightlife
title: Earl Hines as the creator of the jazz idiom
summary: He insists Hines was the forerunner of jazz as blacks know it, separate from folklore like Booga-Rooga.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You have some guys that come up to try to tell you how great a musician is, or he can't play, you know what I mean. "I just don't like him," "He can play the piano /but I just don't like him." This is what they say about me: I talk too much. But I talk because it's my prerogative. I can talk if I want to. I came through the period of jazz from the late teens until today and I like to think that I can have something

to say...that I wasn't just walking ..... a sleep walker... that I know that Earl Hines, you know what I mean, was a great stylist, and that he created, you know what I mean, the jazz idiom as we know it, as blacks know/ He created all of that.

I'm not talking about the folklore, now, I'm not talking about the Blind Lemon Jeffersons and the Boogie-Woogie or Booga-Rooga on the guitar. I'm not talking about that. I'm not talking about Charlie Christian. I'm talking about that forerunner of all of this, that we knew, was Earl Hines.
